alternatives.argument: Assume AC. An integrable adapted real process X is a martingale, submartingale, or supermartingale when E[X_{n+1}|F_n] equals, is at least, or is at most X_n almost surely for each n>=0, respectively. Local argument: Use CE as a class; no canonical representative is chosen by this definition. The definition is the one-step form. The all-m<=n equivalence is supplied by the next lemma, not assumed. The sign convention is sub = future conditional mean >= present. AC is inherited from the Radon–Nikodym construction of conditional expectation; if a sequence of versions is needed, AC selects measurable versions at the countably many times. Identities remain identities of almost-sure classes, without completing the filtration.

Assume AC. For an integrable adapted X, each one-step martingale/submartingale/supermartingale condition is equivalent to the corresponding identity/inequality E[X_n|F_m] =/>=/<= X_m for every 0<=m<=n. Local argument: For m=n, conditioning a known variable gives X_m. For n=m+1 use the hypothesis. Induct on n-m: tower gives E[X_n|F_m]=E[E[X_n|F_{n-1}]|F_m]; positivity transports the last-step inequality, then apply induction. For equality use linearity, or both inequalities. The converse takes n=m+1. All inputs are L1 by assumption and CE preserves L1; each fixed calculation has finitely many null exceptions. AC is inherited from the Radon–Nikodym construction of conditional expectation; if a sequence of versions is needed, AC selects measurable versions at the countably many times. Identities remain identities of almost-sure classes, without completing the filtration.

Assume AC. A martingale difference sequence is a sequence of integrable real variables D_n, n>=1, with D_n F_n-measurable and E[D_n|F_{n-1}]=0 almost surely. Local argument: No D_0 is imposed. The filtration includes F_0 and need not be the natural filtration of the differences. Integrability and past-conditioning are explicit parts of the contract. AC is inherited from the Radon–Nikodym construction of conditional expectation; if a sequence of versions is needed, AC selects measurable versions at the countably many times. Identities remain identities of almost-sure classes, without completing the filtration.

Assume AC. If M is a martingale then D_n=M_n-M_{n-1} is a martingale difference sequence. Conversely, given such D and any integrable F_0-measurable M_0, M_n=M_0+sum_{k=1}^n D_k is a martingale. The constructions are inverse with M_0 fixed. Local argument: Differences are measurable at time n because F_{n-1} is contained in F_n; L1 closure gives integrability. Linearity and conditioning a known M_{n-1} give E[D_n|F_{n-1}]=0. Conversely finite sums are adapted and L1 and have conditional next increment zero; condition the known partial sum to conclude. Telescoping recovers M_n-M_0, and adjacent partial-sum subtraction recovers D_n, proving inverse statements. AC is inherited from the Radon–Nikodym construction of conditional expectation; if a sequence of versions is needed, AC selects measurable versions at the countably many times. Identities remain identities of almost-sure classes, without completing the filtration.

Assume AC. For square-integrable real martingale differences and 1<=i<j, E[D_i D_j]=0. Thus their real L2 inner product is zero; in particular finite sums have second moment equal to the sum of their second moments. Local argument: Cauchy–Schwarz gives E|D_i D_j|<infinity. D_i is F_i-measurable and hence F_{j-1}-measurable. Apply the unbounded integrable-product clause of taking-out to obtain E[D_i D_j|F_{j-1}]=D_i E[D_j|F_{j-1}]=0, then preserve expectation. Also E D_i=0. Expand the square of a finite sum; diagonal terms are L1 and every off-diagonal expectation vanishes. No independence or boundedness of the differences is asserted. AC is inherited from the Radon–Nikodym construction of conditional expectation; if a sequence of versions is needed, AC selects measurable versions at the countably many times. Identities remain identities of almost-sure classes, without completing the filtration.

Assume AC. Let M be a real martingale and phi:R->R finite convex. If phi(M_n) is integrable at every n, then (phi(M_n)) is a submartingale. If instead X is a submartingale and phi is also nondecreasing, the same conclusion holds under the same integrability hypotheses. Local argument: Finite convex phi is Borel by the supporting-line supplier, so compositions are adapted. Conditional Jensen applied to M_{n+1} gives E[phi(M_{n+1})|F_n]>=phi(E[M_{n+1}|F_n])=phi(M_n). The stipulated L1 hypotheses hold at each adjacent time; no convex image of an arbitrary L1 variable is presumed integrable. AC is inherited from the Radon–Nikodym construction of conditional expectation; if a sequence of versions is needed, AC selects measurable versions at the countably many times. Identities remain identities of almost-sure classes, without completing the filtration. For the additional clause, conditional Jensen and monotonicity of phi give E[phi(X_{n+1})|F_n]>=phi(E[X_{n+1}|F_n])>=phi(X_n).

Assume AC. If M is a martingale, |M| is a submartingale. For real p>=1, if E|M_n|^p<infinity at every n, then (|M_n|^p) is a submartingale, with 0^p=0. Local argument: The published absolute-power lemma proves finiteness, Borel measurability and convexity for every real p>=1, including zero and p=1. Apply the convex-transform theorem. At p=1 the martingale definition already gives the needed integrability. For p>1 retain it as an explicit hypothesis; no p<1 claim is made. AC is inherited from the Radon–Nikodym construction of conditional expectation; if a sequence of versions is needed, AC selects measurable versions at the countably many times. Identities remain identities of almost-sure classes, without completing the filtration.

A real process H indexed by n>=1 is predictable when H_n is F_{n-1}-measurable. No time-zero value or integrability is required by predictability alone. Local argument: Predictability is a measurability condition on a specified real sequence. Since the filtration is increasing it implies F_n-measurability at each positive time, but neither boundedness nor integrability follows.

For an adapted integrable real process X and a finite real predictable H, provided H_k(X_k-X_{k-1}) is integrable for every k>=1, define (H dot X)_0=0 and (H dot X)_n=sum_{k=1}^n H_k(X_k-X_{k-1}). For a martingale integrator this is its discrete martingale transform. Local argument: The products are F_k-measurable by measurable arithmetic and the increasing filtration, and are L1 by the domain hypothesis. Consequently the finite sum is adapted and integrable. If |H_k|<=C_k<infinity a.s. with deterministic C_k, the pointwise bound |H_k Delta X_k|<=C_k(|X_k|+|X_{k-1}|) verifies the domain using monotonicity and linearity of the integral; this does not use the later preservation theorem. Changing finitely many representatives changes the finite sum only on a measurable null union. Outside this domain the same algebraic finite sum may exist but is not an integrable transform. For the almost-sure product bound, split off the measurable exceptional null set: its nonnegative integral is zero, so the pointwise estimate on its complement proves the same L1 bound.

Assume AC. If M is a martingale and H is predictable with |H_k|<=C_k a.s. for finite deterministic constants C_k, then H dot M is a martingale starting at zero. Uniformly bounded predictable H is a special case. More generally the conclusion holds whenever all H_k(M_k-M_{k-1}) are integrable, even without timewise bounds. Local argument: The definition verifies product and partial-sum integrability first. The next increment is H_{n+1}(M_{n+1}-M_n); taking-out and the martingale identity give conditional mean zero. The known accumulated sum conditions to itself. This proves the one-step equality with correct index n+1. Only bounds at each fixed time are needed, since each sum is finite. AC is inherited from the Radon–Nikodym construction of conditional expectation; if a sequence of versions is needed, AC selects measurable versions at the countably many times. Identities remain identities of almost-sure classes, without completing the filtration. Under the more general product hypothesis, the same calculation uses the integrable-product clause of taking-out; the transform definition already gives L1 partial sums. Thus conjugate-Lp/Lq assumptions are sufficient by Holder, but are not necessary.

Assume AC. Let X be a submartingale and H>=0 finite real predictable. If E|H_k(X_k-X_{k-1})|<infinity for every k, then H dot X is a submartingale starting at zero. In particular timewise bounded nonnegative H satisfies this. Local argument: The integral domain yields adapted L1 partial sums. Write d_k=E[X_k-X_{k-1}|F_{k-1}]>=0. Taking-out includes the guarantee H_k d_k in L1 from integrability of H_k Delta X_k, even for unbounded H_k. Thus E[Delta(H dot X)_k|F_{k-1}]=H_k d_k>=0. Add the known previous sum. The bounded case follows from the domain estimate already proved in the definition, with no positivity assumption on X. AC is inherited from the Radon–Nikodym construction of conditional expectation; if a sequence of versions is needed, AC selects measurable versions at the countably many times. Identities remain identities of almost-sure classes, without completing the filtration.

Assume AC. For a real martingale M with E M_n^2<infinity for every n, define <M>_0=0 and <M>_n=sum_{k=1}^n E[(M_k-M_{k-1})^2|F_{k-1}]. This is an integrable predictable process with nonnegative increments. Distinguish the adapted optional sum [M]_n=sum_{k=1}^n (M_k-M_{k-1})^2. Local argument: First (a-b)^2<=2a^2+2b^2 makes each squared increment L1; measurable arithmetic supplies measurability. CE yields finite real measurable integrable versions of their conditional means; replace any negative values by zero on their own F_{k-1}-measurable null sets using conditional positivity. Their finite sums are integrable, F_{n-1}-measurable and increasing. Version changes produce the same class at each n. The optional sum is adapted, increasing and integrable too, but is not claimed predictable or equal to the angle bracket. This establishes all well-definedness before the next theorem. AC is inherited from the Radon–Nikodym construction of conditional expectation; if a sequence of versions is needed, AC selects measurable versions at the countably many times. Identities remain identities of almost-sure classes, without completing the filtration.

Assume AC. For every real square-integrable martingale M, M_n^2-<M>_n is a martingale with initial value M_0^2. Also (M_n-M_0)^2-<M>_n is a martingale starting at zero. No deterministic or zero initial-value hypothesis is imposed. Local argument: Put D_n=M_n-M_{n-1}. It is in L2 by (a-b)^2<=2a^2+2b^2, and E[D_n|F_{n-1}]=0 by the differences theorem. Cauchy–Schwarz makes M_{n-1}D_n L1, so the unbounded taking-out theorem gives E[M_{n-1}D_n|F_{n-1}]=0. Expand M_n^2-M_{n-1}^2=2M_{n-1}D_n+D_n^2 and condition. Subtraction of Delta<M>_n=E[D_n^2|F_{n-1}] yields zero conditional drift. The square and bracket terms are adapted L1. For the centered assertion N_n=M_n-M_0 is a square-integrable martingale because M_0 is measurable for every F_n; N_0=0 and Delta N_n=D_n, hence <N>=<M>. Apply the same proved calculation to N. This proves both statements, without inferring one by subtracting an unjustified product martingale. AC is inherited from the Radon–Nikodym construction of conditional expectation; if a sequence of versions is needed, AC selects measurable versions at the countably many times. Identities remain identities of almost-sure classes, without completing the filtration.

Assume AC. For every real square-integrable martingale M and n>=0, E[M_n^2]=E[M_0^2]+E[<M>_n], all terms finite. In particular M_0=0 gives E[M_n^2]=E[<M>_n]. Local argument: The previous theorem gives the martingale Z_n=M_n^2-<M>_n with Z_0=M_0^2. Apply expectation preservation to E[Z_k|F_{k-1}]=Z_{k-1} and induct to obtain E Z_n=E Z_0. Integrability of the bracket and the two squares permits rearranging this equality. At n=0 the bracket is zero, so the base case is exact. AC is inherited from the Radon–Nikodym construction of conditional expectation; if a sequence of versions is needed, AC selects measurable versions at the countably many times. Identities remain identities of almost-sure classes, without completing the filtration.

Assume AC. For independent real integrable Y_k with E Y_k=0, S_0=c and S_n=c+sum_{k=1}^n Y_k form a martingale for F_0={empty,Omega}, F_n=sigma(Y_1,...,Y_n), with c a fixed real constant. Local argument: The generated-sigma-algebra construction gives a filtration and adapted sums. Finite L1 closure establishes integrability. Group independence separates sigma(Y_{n+1}) from sigma(Y_1,...,Y_n); the independent-variable conditioning lemma gives E[Y_{n+1}|F_n]=0. Condition the known S_n and add the next increment. No identical distribution, variance, or infinite-product construction is required: the independent sequence is given. AC is inherited from the Radon–Nikodym construction of conditional expectation; if a sequence of versions is needed, AC selects measurable versions at the countably many times. Identities remain identities of almost-sure classes, without completing the filtration. For fixed n, the sums S_1,...,S_n are measurable functions of Y_1,...,Y_n, and Y_k=S_k-S_{k-1} with S_0=c; minimality of generated sigma-algebras therefore proves equality of these two finite-history sigma-algebras.

Assume AC. For independent real integrable Y_k with E Y_k=1, M_0=1 and M_n=product_{k=1}^n Y_k form a martingale for the filtration generated by the factors. The factors may be signed. Local argument: Measurable arithmetic makes the finite products adapted. Before conditioning, factorization applied to absolute values gives E|M_n|=product_{k=1}^n E|Y_k|<infinity. Group independence and the independent-variable lemma give E[Y_{n+1}|F_n]=1. The unbounded taking-out clause is legitimate because both Y_{n+1} and M_n Y_{n+1}=M_{n+1} are integrable. It yields E[M_{n+1}|F_n]=M_n. At zero the empty product is one. AC is inherited from the Radon–Nikodym construction of conditional expectation; if a sequence of versions is needed, AC selects measurable versions at the countably many times. Identities remain identities of almost-sure classes, without completing the filtration.

Assume AC. Fix a finite horizon N and probability laws P,Q on (Omega,F_N), with Q absolutely continuous with respect to P and a filtration F_0 contained in ... contained in F_N. With L=dQ/dP, Z_n=E_P[L|F_n] is a nonnegative P-martingale and a density of Q restricted to F_n relative to P restricted to F_n, for 0<=n<=N. If F_0 is trivial then Z_0=1. Local argument: RN applies to finite positive Q and P with the common exhaustion Omega. Its density L is real integrable; event positivity and the zero-integral criterion give L>=0 a.s., and testing Omega gives E_P L=1. The conditional-expectation process theorem yields the martingale, and positivity gives Z_n>=0. For A in F_n the defining identity gives integral_A Z_n dP=integral_A L dP=Q(A), proving the restricted density claim. At n=N, conditioning a known L gives Z_N=L; at trivial F_0 the constant 1 satisfies all event tests. One may extend the finite filtration and Z constantly after N merely to fit N_0 notation. No assertion about infinite-horizon absolute continuity or Girsanov is included. AC is inherited from the Radon–Nikodym construction of conditional expectation; if a sequence of versions is needed, AC selects measurable versions at the countably many times. Identities remain identities of almost-sure classes, without completing the filtration.

Assume AC. Start with positive integers r,g red and green balls and reinforce each drawn color by c>=1 balls. The red proportion R_n/(r+g+nc) is a bounded martingale for the draw-history filtration, at every n>=0. Local argument: Construct the infinite draw history without a new product-space prerequisite: on (0,1] with restricted Lebesgue probability, assign the empty history interval (0,1]. Recursively partition each history interval (a,b] into (a,a+p(b-a)] for red and (a+p(b-a),b] for green, where p=(r+c times number of prior reds)/(r+g+nc). Here 0<p<1, so every finite history interval has positive length. There are finitely many intervals at each depth; endpoints and splits are explicit, and every point has one history at every depth. Let F_n be the finite algebra of unions of depth-n intervals; it is a sigma-algebra because it is finite, and refinements make a filtration. On a depth-n interval the conditional red probability is p by the ratio of lengths, checked by integrating its child indicator over each parent and then every union. If I_{n+1} is its red indicator, R_{n+1}=R_n+c I_{n+1}. Hence E[R_{n+1}/(T_n+c)|F_n]=(R_n+c R_n/T_n)/(T_n+c)=R_n/T_n, with T_n=r+g+nc. The proportions are in [0,1], adapted and integrable. Lebesgue existence uses countable choice, supplied by AC. No convergence or beta-limit law is claimed. AC is inherited from the Radon–Nikodym construction of conditional expectation; if a sequence of versions is needed, AC selects measurable versions at the countably many times. Identities remain identities of almost-sure classes, without completing the filtration.

Assume AC. For independent centered real Y_k with finite variances sigma_k^2=E Y_k^2, S_0=0 and S_n=sum_{k=1}^n Y_k satisfy <S>_n=sum_{k=1}^n sigma_k^2, so S_n^2-sum_{k=1}^n sigma_k^2 is a martingale. Local argument: Grouping independence and conditioning give E[Y_{n+1}|F_n]=0, so S is a martingale. Each S_n is L2: repeated (a+b)^2<=2a^2+2b^2 suffices, or the finite square expansion with Cauchy–Schwarz. The square Y_k^2 is measurable relative to sigma(Y_k), independent of F_{k-1}, and integrable; its conditional expectation is the constant sigma_k^2 by the independent-variable lemma. Substitute into the bracket definition and apply the square-minus-bracket theorem. To distinguish the two brackets, take just Y_1 distributed as -1,0,1 with probabilities 1/4,1/2,1/4 and Y_k=0 for k>=2. Then [S]_1=Y_1^2 varies while <S>_1=1/2. This finite witness uses no B item as a supplier. AC is inherited from the Radon–Nikodym construction of conditional expectation; if a sequence of versions is needed, AC selects measurable versions at the countably many times. Identities remain identities of almost-sure classes, without completing the filtration.

Assume AC. Adaptedness, even together with integrability, does not imply the martingale property: X_n=n on the one-point probability space is a counterexample. Local argument: Take the Dirac probability on a singleton and its trivial filtration at all times. X_n is a finite deterministic constant, so it is measurable and integrable at every n. Conditioning fixes constants, and E[X_{n+1}|F_n]=n+1 is different from n on the event Omega of probability one. Thus the failed hypothesis is conditional fairness, not measurability or integrability. AC is inherited from the Radon–Nikodym construction of conditional expectation; if a sequence of versions is needed, AC selects measurable versions at the countably many times. Identities remain identities of almost-sure classes, without completing the filtration.

Assume AC. An unbounded predictable H and a bounded martingale M can have a finite algebraic gain sum that is not integrable, so it cannot be a martingale or belong to the integrable-transform domain. Local argument: Take Omega={(j,e): j>=1, e in {-1,1}} with mass 2^{-j-1} at each point. The nonnegative weighted-Dirac theorem gives a measure; its total mass is sum_{j>=1}2^{-j}=1, by finite geometric sums and their limit. Let F_0=sigma(j) be unions of the two-point j-blocks and F_n=power set for n>=1. Set M_0=0 and M_n=e for n>=1. On each block the two equally weighted signs have zero mean; summing absolutely over unions proves E[e|F_0]=0 by the event definition. Thereafter M is already known, so it is a bounded martingale. Define H_1=2^j and H_k=0 for k>=2; H is finite and predictable. The first algebraic gain is 2^j e, whose absolute expectation equals sum_{j>=1}1=infinity: finite truncations at j<=m have absolute integral m and MCT passes to the limit. Thus it fails precisely the product-integrability domain. Never write a signed conditional expectation of this nonintegrable gain. AC is inherited from the Radon–Nikodym construction of conditional expectation; if a sequence of versions is needed, AC selects measurable versions at the countably many times. Identities remain identities of almost-sure classes, without completing the filtration.

Assume AC. A submartingale need not have nondecreasing sample paths. On the equiprobable two-point space, X_0=0 and X_n=e in {-1,1} for n>=1 give a counterexample. Local argument: Take F_0 trivial and F_n full for n>=1. The first conditional mean is zero by its finite event averages; later the variable is already known. Therefore X is a martingale and in particular a submartingale. On the atom e=-1, of probability 1/2, X_1<X_0. Only conditional mean increments are nonnegative; the Doob compensator may be increasing without the original process being increasing. AC is inherited from the Radon–Nikodym construction of conditional expectation; if a sequence of versions is needed, AC selects measurable versions at the countably many times. Identities remain identities of almost-sure classes, without completing the filtration.

Assume AC. Every integrable adapted X has a unique Doob decomposition up to equality almost surely at each time: A_0=0, A_n=sum_{k=1}^n E[X_k-X_{k-1}|F_{k-1}], M_n=X_n-A_n. The processes may be taken equal outside one common null set for all times when comparing two decompositions. Local argument: Each increment of A is integrable and F_{k-1}-measurable by CE. For k<=n these sigma-algebras lie inside F_{n-1}, so A_n is predictable; finite sums are L1. The difference M=X-A is adapted L1. With Delta A_n already known at time n-1, linearity gives E[Delta M_n|F_{n-1}]=E[Delta X_n|F_{n-1}]-Delta A_n=0. Thus M is a martingale. Conversely any decomposition forces E[Delta X_n|F_{n-1}]=Delta A_n, since Delta M_n has conditional mean zero and Delta A_n is known. Induction from A_0=0 forces A and then M. The countable union of equality-exception sets is measurable and null, establishing simultaneous uniqueness without requiring completeness. AC is inherited from the Radon–Nikodym construction of conditional expectation; if a sequence of versions is needed, AC selects measurable versions at the countably many times. Identities remain identities of almost-sure classes, without completing the filtration.

alternatives.argument: A discrete filtered probability space is (Omega,F,(F_n)_{n>=0},P), where P is a probability measure and F_n are sub-sigma-algebras of F with F_n contained in F_{n+1}. Time is N_0. No completeness or triviality of F_0 is imposed. Local argument: This is a structure, not an existence assertion. Each restriction of P to F_n is a probability measure: the same empty-set, disjoint-union and total-mass identities apply to the smaller sigma-algebra. All processes below are real-valued unless explicitly stated otherwise.

A real stochastic process is a sequence (X_n)_{n>=0} of real random variables on one probability space. It is adapted if X_n is F_n-measurable for every n, and integrable if E|X_n|<infinity for each n. These are separate properties; neither means uniform L1 boundedness. Local argument: Interpret integrability through the ambient Lebesgue expectation and measurability through Borel preimages. The phrase integrable adapted process requires both conditions at every fixed time; there is no assertion about sup_n E|X_n|.

For a real process X, F_n^X is the sigma-algebra generated by all X_k^{-1}(B), 0<=k<=n and B real Borel. This is the smallest filtration making X adapted. Local argument: The ambient F contains each generator. The generated-sigma-algebra theorem supplies a sub-sigma-algebra; inclusion of generator families makes the sequence increasing by minimality. Each X_n is measurable for it. Any filtration making X adapted contains every generator at time n and hence F_n^X. Do not presume that any arbitrary modification on an ambient null set is measurable for F_n^X.

Assume AC. For X in L1(P) and any filtration, M_n=E[X|F_n] is a martingale. Local argument: Each output class has an F_n-measurable integrable version by CE existence. Tower gives E[M_{n+1}|F_n]=E[X|F_n]=M_n. This proves the one-step condition. Versions may be selected at all times under AC, and the countable union of the measurable exceptional sets is null if simultaneous identities are wanted. AC is inherited from the Radon–Nikodym construction of conditional expectation; if a sequence of versions is needed, AC selects measurable versions at the countably many times. Identities remain identities of almost-sure classes, without completing the filtration.

Assume AC. A Doob decomposition of an integrable adapted X is X_n=M_n+A_n, where M is an integrable martingale, A is integrable and predictable for n>=1, and A_0=0. A is called the compensator. Hence M_0=X_0. Local argument: This defines a decomposition if one exists. Existence and uniqueness are discharged by the next theorem, not assumed here. Predictability is asserted for A_n, not merely for an unspecified optional process, and A_0=0 fixes the additive F_0-measurable ambiguity. Equality is at each time almost surely. AC is inherited from the Radon–Nikodym construction of conditional expectation; if a sequence of versions is needed, AC selects measurable versions at the countably many times. Identities remain identities of almost-sure classes, without completing the filtration.

Assume AC. Every integrable adapted X has a unique Doob decomposition up to equality almost surely at each time: A_0=0, A_n=sum_{k=1}^n E[X_k-X_{k-1}|F_{k-1}], M_n=X_n-A_n. The processes may be taken equal outside one common null set for all times when comparing two decompositions. Local argument: Each increment of A is integrable and F_{k-1}-measurable by CE. For k<=n these sigma-algebras lie inside F_{n-1}, so A_n is predictable; finite sums are L1. The difference M=X-A is adapted L1. With Delta A_n already known at time n-1, linearity gives E[Delta M_n|F_{n-1}]=E[Delta X_n|F_{n-1}]-Delta A_n=0. Thus M is a martingale. Conversely any decomposition forces E[Delta X_n|F_{n-1}]=Delta A_n, since Delta M_n has conditional mean zero and Delta A_n is known. Induction from A_0=0 forces A and then M. The countable union of equality-exception sets is measurable and null, establishing simultaneous uniqueness without requiring completeness. AC is inherited from the Radon–Nikodym construction of conditional expectation; if a sequence of versions is needed, AC selects measurable versions at the countably many times. Identities remain identities of almost-sure classes, without completing the filtration.

Assume AC. An integrable adapted X is a submartingale if and only if its Doob compensator satisfies A_n>=A_{n-1} a.s. for every n>=1. Equivalently, A has nondecreasing sample paths outside a single null set. Local argument: The explicit formula gives Delta A_n=E[X_n|F_{n-1}]-X_{n-1}; the right-hand side is nonnegative exactly for a submartingale. For the converse use the same formula or condition X=M+A and the known A_n. Countable subadditivity supplies a common null set for all n. No assertion of monotone sample paths for X follows. AC is inherited from the Radon–Nikodym construction of conditional expectation; if a sequence of versions is needed, AC selects measurable versions at the countably many times. Identities remain identities of almost-sure classes, without completing the filtration.

Assume AC. On (0,1] with Lebesgue probability, partition into I_{n,j}=(j/2^n,(j+1)/2^n], 0<=j<2^n. For f in L1, the dyadic averages M_n=sum_j (2^n integral_{I_{n,j}} f) 1_{I_{n,j}} are conditional expectations and form a martingale for these finite partitions. Local argument: Define F_n to be all unions of the displayed finitely many cells; complement and any union again select cells, so F_n is a sigma-algebra. Each cell splits into two children, giving a filtration. Each cell has measure 2^{-n}>0 by the half-open volume clause of Lebesgue existence; each average is finite. The cellwise constant M_n is F_n-measurable and E|M_n|<=sum_j integral_{I_{n,j}}|f|=E|f|. For a union A of cells, the finite sum gives integral_A M_n=integral_A f. Thus uniqueness identifies the CE class, and the conditional-expectation process theorem proves the martingale. For a concrete calculation f=1_{(0,1/2]}, M_0=1/2 and M_n=f for n>=1. Countable choice for Lebesgue existence follows from AC. There is no convergence assertion or conditioning on points. AC is inherited from the Radon–Nikodym construction of conditional expectation; if a sequence of versions is needed, AC selects measurable versions at the countably many times. Identities remain identities of almost-sure classes, without completing the filtration.

Assume AC. For an integrable adapted X, each one-step martingale/submartingale/supermartingale condition is equivalent to the corresponding identity/inequality E[X_n|F_m] =/>=/<= X_m for every 0<=m<=n. Local argument: For m=n, conditioning a known variable gives X_m. For n=m+1 use the hypothesis. Induct on n-m: tower gives E[X_n|F_m]=E[E[X_n|F_{n-1}]|F_m]; positivity transports the last-step inequality, then apply induction. For equality use linearity, or both inequalities. The converse takes n=m+1. All inputs are L1 by assumption and CE preserves L1; each fixed calculation has finitely many null exceptions. AC is inherited from the Radon–Nikodym construction of conditional expectation; if a sequence of versions is needed, AC selects measurable versions at the countably many times. Identities remain identities of almost-sure classes, without completing the filtration.

Assume AC. For independent real integrable Y_k with E Y_k=0, S_0=c and S_n=c+sum_{k=1}^n Y_k form a martingale for F_0={empty,Omega}, F_n=sigma(Y_1,...,Y_n), with c a fixed real constant. Local argument: The generated-sigma-algebra construction gives a filtration and adapted sums. Finite L1 closure establishes integrability. Group independence separates sigma(Y_{n+1}) from sigma(Y_1,...,Y_n); the independent-variable conditioning lemma gives E[Y_{n+1}|F_n]=0. Condition the known S_n and add the next increment. No identical distribution, variance, or infinite-product construction is required: the independent sequence is given. AC is inherited from the Radon–Nikodym construction of conditional expectation; if a sequence of versions is needed, AC selects measurable versions at the countably many times. Identities remain identities of almost-sure classes, without completing the filtration. For fixed n, the sums S_1,...,S_n are measurable functions of Y_1,...,Y_n, and Y_k=S_k-S_{k-1} with S_0=c; minimality of generated sigma-algebras therefore proves equality of these two finite-history sigma-algebras.

Assume AC. Let M be a real martingale and phi:R->R finite convex. If phi(M_n) is integrable at every n, then (phi(M_n)) is a submartingale. If instead X is a submartingale and phi is also nondecreasing, the same conclusion holds under the same integrability hypotheses. Local argument: Finite convex phi is Borel by the supporting-line supplier, so compositions are adapted. Conditional Jensen applied to M_{n+1} gives E[phi(M_{n+1})|F_n]>=phi(E[M_{n+1}|F_n])=phi(M_n). The stipulated L1 hypotheses hold at each adjacent time; no convex image of an arbitrary L1 variable is presumed integrable. AC is inherited from the Radon–Nikodym construction of conditional expectation; if a sequence of versions is needed, AC selects measurable versions at the countably many times. Identities remain identities of almost-sure classes, without completing the filtration. For the additional clause, conditional Jensen and monotonicity of phi give E[phi(X_{n+1})|F_n]>=phi(E[X_{n+1}|F_n])>=phi(X_n).

Assume AC. If M is a martingale and H is predictable with |H_k|<=C_k a.s. for finite deterministic constants C_k, then H dot M is a martingale starting at zero. Uniformly bounded predictable H is a special case. More generally the conclusion holds whenever all H_k(M_k-M_{k-1}) are integrable, even without timewise bounds. Local argument: The definition verifies product and partial-sum integrability first. The next increment is H_{n+1}(M_{n+1}-M_n); taking-out and the martingale identity give conditional mean zero. The known accumulated sum conditions to itself. This proves the one-step equality with correct index n+1. Only bounds at each fixed time are needed, since each sum is finite. AC is inherited from the Radon–Nikodym construction of conditional expectation; if a sequence of versions is needed, AC selects measurable versions at the countably many times. Identities remain identities of almost-sure classes, without completing the filtration. Under the more general product hypothesis, the same calculation uses the integrable-product clause of taking-out; the transform definition already gives L1 partial sums. Thus conjugate-Lp/Lq assumptions are sufficient by Holder, but are not necessary.
